summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework: federal law criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity across the country, and the state layer adds Sharia offences that reach Muslims alone. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code, in force in Johor, punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping. The provisions cover oral and anal sex, apply to men and women alike, reach acts that are consensual and private, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens.

Johor's Sharia enactment sits alongside that federal layer, prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females" together with liwat and musahaqah, with penalties under the national framework reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences apply only to Muslims; a non-Muslim visitor falls under the federal Penal Code alone. Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, leaving the line between compliant and offending presentation to officers on the ground.

In November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The stated purpose is the reorientation of the visitor-facing presentation of gender and sexuality through state-run institutions, and a visitor detained under either layer could in principle be routed into such a programme.

Nationally, at least 1,733 people had attended "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown running since the 2018 election. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters documented state-conducted investigations spanning Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, confirming that the campaign is a pattern across the country rather than a single state's policy.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable. Identity documents remain controlled by the state: the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and the 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holding that sex is determined at birth is applied in practice even though it was never gazetted and is not legally binding.

There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors, but entry policy is not neutral in practice; the nearest documented statement is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but that discretion is not a legal protection and has been withdrawn at moments of political pressure.
tangentialFactors:
Venue-based policing is the most visible front of enforcement. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022; media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published, and 17 civil servants identified among the arrestees were suspended. A magistrate rejected the request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Similar raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and 11 shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches; after the Home Minister said on 2 December 2025 that the provisions would be revisited, police raided another sauna in Penang within days.

Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented over decades, including repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times, a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention. Violence against transgender women is lethal and largely unpunished: a trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing in Malaysia in fewer than two months, and reporting on those killings is obstructed.

Legal challenges have failed to remove the framework. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised. Custodial alternatives prescribed by the Sharia enactments include commitment to an approved home for up to six months and counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution.
localsOnly:
Johor residents who are Muslim face the Sharia layer in addition to the federal Penal Code, including cross-dressing and "males posing as females" offences punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, an RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning. The state Islamic religious department conducts enforcement, and presentation-based arrests are made without a statutory definition of transgender dress to test them against.

The Johor government's November 2023 announcement of conversion-therapy centres sits within a national programme that had enrolled at least 1,733 people in "rehabilitation programmes" by June 2021, running under a crackdown that began after the 2018 election. Residents detained under either legal layer are the population those centres are intended to receive.

Gender-marker changes on identity documents are refused by the Registration Department in practice. The 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict that sex is fixed at birth was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but is applied, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. A 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court order requiring the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoned from the Federal Constitution's guarantee of a right to live with dignity in one's gender, was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

No anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection exists on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and same-sex marriage and partner recognition are unavailable. Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and order other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months, extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state whether conversion-therapy centres announced for Johor in November 2023 have been built, opened, or are operating, and no figures are given for participants in Johor specifically. The national total of 1,733 rehabilitation-programme attendees as of June 2021 is not broken down by state.

No Johor-specific enforcement statistics, arrest counts or dates are sourced here; the raid and arrest evidence in the record comes from Kuala Lumpur, Penang and other states and is used to indicate the national pattern a visitor in Johor stands under. Whether Johor's religious department has conducted venue raids of the kind seen elsewhere is unresolved in this inventory.

The precise text of Johor's Sharia enactment and its current amendment status are not quoted in these sources beyond the national penalty ceiling. The inventory also does not resolve whether the 1982 fatwa is applied by Johor's own authorities or how Johor's Registration Department handles marker-change requests in practice.
